title: One written word read as two different words: three cases or four?
issue: Chapter 2 of the MAM Introduction counts three cases; the Introduction’s template appendix counts four and includes 2 Samuel 8:3.
context: Ketiv is the written form; qere is what is read aloud. This category is a single written word assigned two spoken words whose letters differ from the written form, rather than merely splitting that form at a space. The appendix lists 2 Samuel 8:3, Ezekiel 9:11, 2 Kings 18:27 and Isaiah 36:12.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — “Qere differs from ketiv in two words”
panels.quote: בשלושה פסוקים במקרא יש הערת "קרי" המייחסת שתי מילים של "קרי" למילה אחת של "כתיב".
panels.translation: In three verses in Scripture there is a qere note assigning two qere words to one ketiv word.

panels.label: Introduction, appendix — “List of templates for documentation and layout”
panels.quote: (2 פריטים מתוך 4 הערות מסורה):''' [[שמואל ב ח/טעמים#ח ג|שמ"ב ח,ג]] (בנהר > בנהר פרת); [[יחזקאל ט/טעמים#ט יא|יחזקאל ט,יא]] (כאשר > ככל אשר).
panels.translation: Two items out of four Masorah notes: 2 Samuel 8:3 (בנהר → בנהר פרת, “at the river” → “at the River Euphrates”); Ezekiel 9:11 (כאשר → ככל אשר, “as” → “according to all that”).

panels.label: Doc-note, 2 Samuel 8:3 — Aleppo reading
panels.quote: א-קרי="בנהר פרת" (שתי התיבות), אמנם חסרים המקף לתיבה "בנהר", והרווח והניקוד לתיבה "פְּרָֽת" שאינה נכתבת.
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex qere: “בנהר פרת” (“at the River Euphrates”), both words; however, the maqaf for “בנהר” is missing, as are the space and pointing for “פְּרָֽת”, which is not written.

panels.label: Current MAM reading, 2 Samuel 8:3
panels.translation: At the River Euphrates.

explanation: The chapter 2 list omits 2 Samuel 8:3. The appendix and the current MAM template include it in this category, and its note explains the two-word Aleppo qere. The other manuscript traditions treat the final word as a separate “read but not written” item, so a count of traditional Masorah notes could depend on the intended convention.
decision: Decide whether chapter 2 is meant to count the four cases used by MAM’s template appendix. If so, it needs 2 Samuel 8:3 and a total of four. If it is counting a narrower manuscript convention, state that convention and explain why Samuel is excluded.

title: Jeremiah 31:37 — which mark is attributed to Aleppo?
issue: The Introduction quotes an etnahta on the divine name; the doc-note’s Aleppo quotation has a meteg at that position.
context: The phrase is “days [are coming], says the LORD.” “Are coming” is read aloud but has no written consonants in this ketiv. Both passages say its intended gap lacks pointing; the disagreement concerns the mark on the following divine name.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — missing pointing for qere without ketiv
panels.quote: (א-כתיב=יָמִ֥ים [֯] נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה): חסר ניקוד ברווח המיועד ל"בָּאִ֖ים" (קרי ולא כתיב)
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex ketiv: “days [gap], says the LORD.” Pointing is missing in the space intended for “בָּאִ֖ים” (“are coming”, read but not written).

panels.label: Doc-note, Jeremiah 31:37 — Aleppo quotation
panels.quote: א=הִנֵּ֛ה יָמִ֥ים [] נְאֻם־יְהֹוָֽה (חסר ניקוד ברווח המיועד ל"קרי ולא כתיב")
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex reads: “Behold, days [gap], says the LORD” (pointing is missing in the space intended for the word read but not written).

explanation: The visible forms attribute different marks to the same manuscript. The current MAM reading has etnahta, like the Introduction, but an edition’s chosen reading does not settle what Aleppo contains. The doc-note also includes a holam that the Introduction quotation omits; that is a separate quotation-policy question. The vertical mark here is mid-verse meteg, not verse-final silluq.
decision: Determine which Aleppo quotation is intended, then reconcile the two attributed forms. This comparison alone does not establish the physical manuscript reading.

reading_forms.gloss: “Says the LORD”; etnahta on the divine name.

reading_forms.label: Doc-note: meteg
reading_forms.gloss: “Says the LORD”; meteg on the divine name.

title: Numbers 9:7 — the note names vav, but the added letter is yod
issue: The doc-note calls the selected spelling “full vav”; the displayed word contains a yod and no vav.
context: People unable to bring the Passover offering ask why they are prevented from “offering” it. The two spellings of “offer” differ by the yod before the final bet.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3 — Torah spelling differences
panels.translation: MAM: הַקְרִ֜יב (“offer”), with yod; Leningrad Codex: הַקְרִ֜ב, without yod. The asterisk marks the form selected for MAM.

panels.label: Word annotated by the doc-note, Numbers 9:7
panels.translation: Offer — the selected spelling includes yod.

panels.label: Doc-note — description of the selected spelling
panels.translation: (Spelling with vav included.)

panels.label: Doc-note — Leningrad alternative
panels.translation: Leningrad Codex reads הַקְרִ֜ב (“offer”), with yod omitted.

explanation: The Introduction and both word forms distinguish presence or absence of yod. The doc-note’s phrase “full vav” names the wrong letter: its selected form has no vav. This is a note-side wording error, not evidence that either manuscript spelling needs to change.
decision: Change the selected-spelling description from vav to yod if these are the intended forms. No manuscript interpretation is needed to identify this letter-name mismatch.

title: Deuteronomy 32:34 — the note names yod, but the added letter is vav
issue: The doc-note calls the selected spelling “full yod”; its word contains vav and no yod.
context: The word means “sealed” in “sealed up in my treasuries.” MAM and Leningrad differ by the vav that carries the shuruq vowel.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3 — Torah spelling differences
panels.translation: MAM selects חָת֖וּם (“sealed”), with vav; Leningrad Codex reads חָתֻ֖ם, without vav.

panels.label: Word annotated by the doc-note
panels.translation: Sealed — includes vav.

panels.label: Doc-note — selected-spelling description
panels.translation: (Spelling with yod included.)

panels.label: Doc-note — Leningrad alternative
panels.translation: Leningrad Codex surprisingly reads חָתֻ֖ם (“sealed”), with vav omitted.

explanation: The words and the Introduction agree on the vav difference. The selected-spelling description names yod instead. The != operator still means that Leningrad reads the quoted word; it adds a note of surprise.
decision: Reconcile the selected-spelling description with its word: vav, rather than yod, is the relevant letter.

title: Deuteronomy 6:21 — Leningrad is assigned both spellings
issue: The doc-note lists Leningrad among witnesses to the spelling without vav, then explicitly assigns it the spelling with vav.
context: The word means “and he brought us out,” in the account of the exodus from Egypt. The disputed vav follows the initial yod.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3 — Torah spelling differences
panels.translation: MAM selects וַיֹּצִיאֵ֧נוּ (“and he brought us out”), without that vav; Leningrad Codex reads וַיּוֹצִיאֵ֧נוּ, with it.

panels.label: Doc-note — beginning of the agreement list
panels.translation: MAM agrees with Leningrad Codex and St Petersburg, Firkovich B 17. The rest of this clause lists further witnesses; its spelling description says vav is omitted.

panels.label: Doc-note — explicit Leningrad alternative
panels.translation: Leningrad Codex surprisingly reads וַיּוֹצִיאֵ֧נוּ (“and he brought us out”), with vav included.

panels.label: Doc-note — concluding manuscript statement
panels.translation: Sassoon Codex 507: vav omitted; Leningrad Codex: vav included.

explanation: A leading = identifies agreement with the word selected in MAM, which lacks the vav. Thus the first clause assigns Leningrad a different spelling from the explicit alternative and the concluding prose. The Introduction agrees with the latter two clauses.
decision: Reconcile Leningrad’s entry in the initial witness list with the note’s explicit spelling and concluding explanation. This is an internal attribution inconsistency in the note; the cache comparison does not independently inspect the manuscript.

title: Deuteronomy’s list of hataf vowels on non-guttural letters
issue: The Introduction labels this list “9 items,” but it names eleven verses and twelve words.
context: The list identifies exceptional hataf vowels — short composite vowels — on letters that are not guttural. The first six entries cite Leningrad Codex; the last five cite Aleppo Codex. Deuteronomy 32:10 supplies two words in a single verse.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3 — heading of the Deuteronomy list
panels.translation: (9 items.)

panels.label: Introduction — the entry containing two words
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex: יְסֹבֲבֶ֙נְהוּ֙ (“he surrounds him”), יְב֣וֹנֲנֵ֔הוּ (“he cares for him”).

panels.label: Doc-note, Deuteronomy 32:10
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex reads the two quoted words (“he surrounds him; he cares for him”), with a hataf vowel in each.

explanation: The eleven verse entries are 5:23; 8:2, 8:15; 15:20, 15:22; 24:13; 28:39; 29:7; 32:10, 32:18 and 32:36. The associated notes support the listed manuscript readings. Neither counting verses nor counting words produces nine.
decision: Choose the intended counting unit and update the heading accordingly: eleven verse entries or twelve words. List completeness beyond these entries remains a separate question.

title: Lamentations 1:6 — “one word” and “two words” are reversed
issue: The Introduction’s definition says two written words are read as one, but its Lamentations example describes the opposite.
context: The phrase means “from the daughter [of Zion].” The written words are מִן בַּת־; the spoken word is מִבַּת־. The final maqaf joins the following word and does not turn the two space-separated written words into one.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — definition of “two written words, one read word”
panels.quote: "כתיב תרתין מילין וקרי מילה חדה", כלומר: "כתיב" שהוא שתי מילים אבל ה"קרי" שלו מילה אחת.
panels.translation: “Two written words and one read word”: that is, a ketiv of two words whose qere is one word.

panels.label: Introduction, same section — Lamentations 1:6 example
panels.quote: ("מִן בַּת־" כתיב בתיבה אחת, "מִבַּת־" קרי בשתי תיבות).
panels.translation: (“מִן בַּת־”, “from the daughter,” is written as one word; “מִבַּת־”, “from the daughter,” is read as two words.)

explanation: The example’s labels reverse the section’s definition and the visible word separation. The parsed ketiv/qere structure also encodes two written words and one spoken word. There is no doc-note at this verse; this is an internal Introduction wording discrepancy.
decision: Reverse “one” and “two” in the example’s descriptions if the displayed words are intended.

title: Proverbs 30:19 — the illustration drops a retained maqaf
issue: The Introduction’s MAM illustration spaces “on the rock”; the current MAM word is joined by maqaf, as the note attributes to Aleppo.
context: The phrase describes “the way of a snake on the rock.” Maqaf is the horizontal joining mark between the two Hebrew words.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — displayed MAM words
panels.translation: On the rock — shown with a space.

panels.label: Introduction, same illustration — Aleppo note
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex reads עֲלֵ֫י־צ֥וּר (“on the rock”), with maqaf.

panels.label: Current MAM words annotated by the doc-note
panels.translation: On the rock — joined by maqaf.

panels.label: Doc-note, Proverbs 30:19
panels.translation: MAM agrees with Aleppo Codex (with maqaf). Printed editions read עֲלֵ֫י צ֥וּר (“on the rock”), with a space.

explanation: The Introduction’s own Aleppo quotation agrees with the current note and current MAM text. The mismatch is in the illustrated edition text, which instead displays the spaced printed-edition reading.
decision: Reconcile the Introduction’s MAM illustration with the retained maqaf. These passages do not establish competing Aleppo readings.

title: Aleppo’s omitted oleh mark — eleven poetic verses or thirteen?
issue: Chapter 2 says eleven verses; the chapter 5 list to which it refers says thirteen.
context: The oleh and yored marks together constitute a poetic accent. These passages concern cases where Aleppo places the yored mark on a letter but omits the accompanying oleh mark, which MAM supplies.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — discussion of oleh and yored
panels.quote: בכתר ארם צובה יש השמטה שיטתית ועקבית כזאת של ה"עולה" ב-11 פסוקי אמ"ת
panels.translation: In the Aleppo Codex there is this systematic, consistent omission of the oleh mark in eleven poetic verses.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — “Oleh and yored on one letter”
panels.quote: להלן רשימה של כל פסוקי אמ"ת (סה"כ 13) שבהם סימנו "עולה ויורד" באופן מלא (=תו של "עולה" ותו של "יורד") באות אחת
panels.translation: Below is a list of all poetic verses (thirteen in total) in which we marked oleh and yored in full — an oleh mark and a yored mark — on one letter.

panels.label: One listed example: doc-note, Psalm 68:20
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex reads י֥וֹם (“day”), omitting the oleh mark.

explanation: The chapter 5 list contains seven Psalms verses (30:12; 42:3; 55:20; 68:20; 86:2; 109:16; 125:2), two Proverbs verses (24:24; 30:15) and four Job verses (8:6; 9:22; 29:25; 34:20). These are thirteen distinct verses, not eleven. Their local note relationships were checked separately.
decision: Reconcile chapter 2’s count with chapter 5’s thirteen entries, or explain any intended exclusion. This does not independently prove manuscript-wide completeness.

title: Isaiah’s four editorial decisions — which categories contain them?
issue: The Introduction calls four cases “the first three types,” but its preceding list puts four cases in the first two types.
context: The section “Isaiah as an example of applying the method” divides unusual readings into five types. Type 1 is a doubtful letter at Isaiah 10:15; type 2 contains three pointing or accent questions. Type 3 adds two separate pointing anomalies.

panels.quote: ספק קל לגבי קביעת אות אחת בכתר:

panels.quote: ספקות בקביעת הניקוד והטעמים והגעיות בכתר (3 מקומות
panels.translation: Doubts in establishing the vowels, accents and meteg marks in the Aleppo Codex (three places

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — type 3
panels.quote: מקומות חריגים בשיטת הניקוד בכתר (2 מקומות).
panels.translation: Unusual cases in the Aleppo Codex’s pointing system (two places).

panels.label: Introduction — introduction to the four decisions
panels.quote: לגבי שלושת הסוגים הראשונים (כלומר ארבעת המקומות בספר ישעיהו
panels.translation: Regarding the first three types (that is, the four places in the book of Isaiah

explanation: The first two types contain 1 + 3 = 4 places. The first three contain 1 + 3 + 2 = 6. The four decisions that follow concern Isaiah 10:15, 55:5, 45:6 and 14:2, matching the first two types. This is a grouping description error, rather than a reconsideration of the editorial decisions.
decision: Determine whether “first two types” is the intended wording; the listed decisions support that reading.

title: The appendix’s completion date — 7 Tevet 5774 or 10 December 2014?
issue: The Hebrew and Gregorian dates printed for the end of a round of corrections fall in different years.
context: This is the Introduction appendix’s account of work on the edition, especially the doc-notes. It is a date-label comparison; it does not establish when that work actually ended.

panels.label: Introduction, appendix — stated completion date
panels.translation: Ended on 7 Tevet 5774 (10 December 2014).

explanation: 7 Tevet 5774 corresponds to 10 December 2013. Conversely, 10 December 2014 corresponds to 18 Kislev 5775. The local calendar conversions round-trip, so the stated pair cannot name one date.
decision: Use the historical evidence to decide which date is intended, then make the other calendar date agree. Do not choose the event date from this mismatch alone.

title: Job 9:10 — chapter and verse reversed in an example

context: The example concerns an early geresh accent on the initial letter of וְנִפְלָא֗וֹת, “and wonders.” The intended verse speaks of great deeds and wonders beyond counting.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 1 — named reference and word
panels.translation: For example: in Job 10:9, the word וְנִפְלָא֗וֹת (“and wonders”)

title: Westminster transcription notes — version 4.14 or 4.16?
issue: The Introduction introduces a quotation as version 4.14, but the quoted heading names version 4.16.
context: The page “Differences in the Westminster transcription” reproduces a historical legend explaining its transcription-note categories. Version matters because the categories and their totals describe a particular release.

panels.quote: פירושם של כל ההערות בהקלדת וסטמינסטר בגירסה 4.14:

panels.translation: Transcription notes in the Westminster Leningrad Codex [4.16].

Its arithmetic is internally consistent, but that does not resolve which release the Hebrew introduction is intended to identify. The current repository’s Westminster 4.22 copy is a different release and cannot settle this historical label.

title: Daily seder reading — a Hebrew year or a solar year?
issue: The chapter 5 explanation says an ordinary Hebrew year; the Koren passage it quotes explicitly calculates a 365-day solar year.
context: A seder is a marked reading division. This passage proposes daily reading as an explanation for the 293 divisions in Prophets and Writings, excluding Sabbaths and festivals. The Introduction acknowledges that the original reason for the division is unknown.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — division into sedarim in Prophets and Writings
panels.quote: מספר הסדרים קרוב או זהה למספר ימי החול בשנה עברית רגילה (למעט שבתות ומועדים).
panels.translation: The number of sedarim is close to or identical with the number of weekdays in an ordinary Hebrew year (excluding Sabbaths and festivals).

panels.label: Introduction, same section — quotation from the Koren preface
panels.quote: סיכומם של ימות החול (293) וימי שבת וחג (71) הוא 364, כלומר, מנין ימיה של שנת השמש חסר יום אחד
panels.translation: The sum of weekdays (293) and Sabbath and festival days (71) is 364: that is, the number of days in a solar year less one day.

explanation: The quotation excludes the remaining day, Tisha be-Av, to reach 365. Its arithmetic is consistent; the tension is the narrative’s Hebrew-year description versus the quotation’s solar-year description. These are two passages inside the Introduction, not an Introduction/doc-note disagreement.
decision: Decide which calendar description the explanation intends. Clarify the narrative or its relation to the quoted proposal before treating it as a historical claim.

title: 2 Kings 18:27 — the Aleppo ketiv’s shin dot
issue: The Introduction’s Aleppo quotation includes a shin dot that the doc-note’s Aleppo quotation omits.
context: The ketiv word is read aloud as “water of their feet,” the euphemism in the Rabshakeh’s speech. This comparison concerns the shin dot on the written word, rather than how its two-word qere is laid out.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — Aleppo ketiv
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex ketiv: the quoted written word, with a shin dot.

panels.label: Doc-note, 2 Kings 18:27 — Aleppo ketiv
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex ketiv: two ways of displaying the same unusual pointing, both without the shin dot. The plus sign separates superimposed pointing for font display.

explanation: The current text of issue #305 records Ben’s conclusion that the doc-note was correct. This audit preserves that tracked result separately from its new comparisons and has not inspected a manuscript scan.
decision: Use #305 for the existing correction; no new manuscript decision is raised here.

panels.label: Doc-note, Ezekiel 14:14 — Aleppo ketiv

panels.translation: Aleppo Codex ketiv: “Daniel” (hiriq, tsere and munah below the dageshed nun, in that order).

title: Psalm 108:11: tipeha or dehi in “lead me”
issue: The Introduction’s Aleppo specimen has tipeha, while the note’s quotation attributed to Breuer has dehi.
context: The speaker asks who will lead him to the fortified city; the disputed word means “lead me.” Both sources discuss whether its nun has a dagesh, but their accent marks also differ.

panels.label: Introduction, Chapter 5: unusual pointing in Psalms
panels.translation: Possible Aleppo reading: “lead me”; does the nun have a dagesh?

panels.label: Psalm 108:11 note: Breuer’s Aleppo reading
panels.quote: לפי ברויאר א=יֹ֭בִלֵנִּי (נו"ן דגושה) אבל לא כך נראה בכתב־היד בהגדלה (אמנם המקום קצת מטושטש).
panels.translation: According to Breuer, Aleppo has “lead me” with a dagesh in nun, but the enlarged manuscript does not appear to have this, although the area is somewhat blurred.

explanation: The nun-dagesh question is shared. The separate difference is the accent near the beginning: tipeha in the Introduction, dehi in the note’s Breuer quotation.
decision: Should the Introduction specimen have dehi, matching the note’s Breuer quotation, or is its tipeha intentional?

title: Psalm 57:9: dehi or terha in the alternative reading of “awake!”
issue: The Introduction’s second possible Aleppo reading has dehi and merkha, whereas the note’s alternative has terha and merkha.
context: The disputed occurrence of “awake!” introduces the harp and lyre. Both sources prefer a reading with dehi and a meteg that indicates stress.

reading_forms.label: Current MAM reading, attributed to Leningrad

title: 2 Samuel 21:12 — one reading note for two words or three?
issue: Does the chapter 5 entry intentionally discuss only the last two words, or should it describe the three words covered by the reading note?
context: David retrieves Saul and Jonathan’s bones from Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them. The disputed group means ‘the Philistines hung them there.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — the 2 Samuel 21:12 entry
panels.quote: (א-כתיב=שָׁםָּ ה֙פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים): הערת קרי אחת לשתי התיבות
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex written form: ‘there, the Philistines.’ One qere reading note covers the two words.

panels.label: Introduction, appendices — the template for three words in one reading note
panels.translation: Three words in one note.

panels.label: Local note on the complete three-word group
panels.quote: א-קרי=<תלאום שמה פלשתים> (הערת קרי אחת לשלוש תיבות ביחד), וכך גם בכתי"ש1.
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex qere: ‘the Philistines hung them there.’ One reading note covers all three words together; Sassoon 1053 has the same arrangement.

panels.label: Introduction, appendix — catalogue of two words under one note
panels.quote: (9 הערות מסורה):''' [[שמואל א כ/טעמים#כ ב|שמ"א כ,ב]]; [[שמואל ב ה/טעמים#ה ב|שמ"ב ה,ב]]; [[שמואל ב כא/טעמים#כא יב|שמ"ב כא,יב]] (מיד אחרי עוד אחד)
panels.translation: Nine Masorah notes: 1 Samuel 20:2; 2 Samuel 5:2; 2 Samuel 21:12 (immediately after another one).

The narrower quotation could explain the chapter’s wording, but that scope is not stated. The appendix also includes this verse in its nine-item two-word-note catalogue, as well as its three-word catalogue. Current MAM uses one three-word template here and has eight two-word templates. The note describes different two-note arrangements in Cairo and Leningrad, so a historical manuscript count and MAM’s current template count need not count the same objects.
decision: Decide whether chapter 5 is describing a two-word subset or the complete reading note. If it is the subset, say so; if it is the complete note, describe all three words. State which manuscript arrangement or MAM template population the appendix’s two-word catalogue is intended to count.

reading_forms.label: Complete pointed reading in the local note

panels.label: Introduction, Summary — phonetic features
panels.quote: מאפיינים אלה אינם מופיעים עדיין בוויקיטקסט
panels.translation: These features do not yet appear on Wikisource.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — current implementation of poetic stress helpers
panels.quote: לגבי טעם הצינור, שאין בו קושי, הטעם הכפול כבר מופיע במהודרתנו

title: Psalm 66:12 — a space in a list headed ‘maqaf’
issue: Is ‘you let them ride’ included as an example of meteg after the accent rather than as an example of maqaf?
context: The verse says that God let people ride over the speakers’ heads. The boundary in question is between the verb ‘you let them ride’ and ‘people.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — heading of the maqaf list
panels.quote: להלן רשימה של כל המקומות בכ"א הספרים שבהם מופיע מקף בתיבת משרת בכתר ובמהדורתנו
panels.translation: Below is a list of all places in the Twenty-one Books where a word with a conjunctive accent has a maqaf in the Aleppo Codex and in our edition.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — the poetic continuation of the same list
panels.translation: And in the Three Books: Psalms, Proverbs, and Job.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — Psalm 66:12 entry in that list
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex: ‘you let them ride.’

explanation: The quoted verb has merkha and a following meteg, but no maqaf. The current verse also has a space after this verb. Its local note concerns another word, so it supplies no Aleppo reading for this boundary. The list may include a broader group of meteg examples than its heading says.
decision: Clarify whether the list includes meteg examples without maqaf. If maqaf is essential to its scope, identify the basis for including this verse.

title: Psalm 119:90 — ‘you established’ in the same maqaf list
issue: Is ‘you established’ included for its meteg rather than for a maqaf after it?
context: The verse says, ‘You established the earth, and it stands.’ The boundary is between ‘you established’ and ‘earth.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — heading of the maqaf list
panels.quote: להלן רשימה של כל המקומות בכ"א הספרים שבהם מופיע מקף בתיבת משרת בכתר ובמהדורתנו
panels.translation: Below is a list of all places in the Twenty-one Books where a word with a conjunctive accent has a maqaf in the Aleppo Codex and in our edition.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — the poetic continuation of the same list
panels.translation: And in the Three Books: Psalms, Proverbs, and Job.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — Psalm 119:90 entry in that list
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex: ‘you established.’

explanation: The example has merkha and a following meteg, but no maqaf. The current verse has a space before ‘earth.’ The local note discusses the accents on ‘earth,’ not this boundary. The heading may need to distinguish examples with maqaf from examples of meteg after the accent.
decision: State the intended reason for including this example. Retain it under a broader heading, or supply the evidence that makes it a maqaf example.

title: 2 Samuel 16:23 — which manuscript has the unpointed gap?
issue: Does the local note’s description of a narrow gap and an unpointed ‘man’ refer specifically to the Aleppo Codex?
context: Ahithophel’s advice is compared with someone asking God for counsel. The read word ‘man’ has no corresponding written word at this position.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — Aleppo’s written form at 2 Samuel 16:23
panels.quote: (א-כתיב=יִשְׁאַל־֯ ): יש רווח צר בלבד ואין ניקוד לתיבה "אִ֖ישׁ" הנקראת ולא נכתבת
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex written form: ‘would ask—’. There is only a narrow gap, and no pointing for ‘man,’ which is read but not written.

panels.label: Local note on the gap and read word
panels.quote: יש רווח צר בלבד ואין ניקוד לתיבה "אִ֖ישׁ" הנקראת ולא נכתבת.
panels.translation: There is only a narrow gap, and no pointing for ‘man,’ which is read but not written.

explanation: The descriptions agree word for word, but only the Introduction names the Aleppo Codex. The local note does not name a manuscript. Its agreement confirms the description, without independently identifying the source.
decision: Confirm that this note is intended as an Aleppo description, preferably with the source of the recorded reading. Until then, distinguish the Introduction’s attribution from the unnamed local description.

reading_forms.label: The word read but not written

title: 2 Kings 14:7 — the missing pashta helper is confirmed; the written pointing is not

context: The verse concerns the defeat of Edom in the Valley of Salt. The written spelling includes an initial he; the read word is ‘salt.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — first entry for the written form
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex written form: ‘the salt’; qere: ‘salt.’ The pashta sign marking the earlier stressed syllable is missing, contrary to its usual practice.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — repeated entry for the written form
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex written form: ‘—the salt’; qere: ‘salt.’ The pashta sign marking the earlier stressed syllable is missing, contrary to its usual practice.

panels.label: Local note explicitly naming Aleppo
panels.translation: The Aleppo Codex unexpectedly has ‘salt’ without the pashta sign on the earlier stressed syllable, contrary to its usual practice.

explanation: The local note explicitly confirms the missing additional pashta sign in Aleppo. That part is resolved. It quotes the read word, however, while the written form in the note’s text is unpointed. It does not supply a complete pointed Aleppo written form with the initial he.
decision: Describe the confirmed omission separately from the written spelling. If the Introduction is intended as a complete pointed written quotation, identify its source.

reading_forms.label: Aleppo read form quoted by the note

title: 2 Kings 18:27 — the source of the pointed written and read forms
issue: What recorded source supports the Aleppo written and read forms quoted for ‘their excrement’?
context: Rabshakeh threatens the people on the wall with conditions in which they would eat their excrement and drink their urine. This question concerns the first expression.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — written and read forms at 2 Kings 18:27
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex written form: ‘their excrement’; qere: ‘their excrement.’ Compare Isaiah 36:12.

explanation: The Introduction explicitly attributes both pointed forms to Aleppo. The current text has the written/read pair, but there is no local note on that pair giving the quoted Aleppo pointing. The verse’s other notes concern Rabshakeh’s name and the separate expression ‘their urine’; their Aleppo attributions cannot establish this reading.
decision: Identify an attributed description or source for this pair. Otherwise state that the pointing is quoted by the Introduction but not independently supplied by its local note.

title: Genesis 36:13 — both descriptions say merkha, but the signs are munah
issue: Should the descriptions name munah, or are the quoted accent signs themselves wrong?
context: The verse lists Reuel’s sons and then says ‘these are the sons of Basemath.’ The disputed word is ‘these.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3 — Genesis 36:13
panels.quote: (ל!=אֵ֣לֶּ֣ה): טעם מרכא פעמיים באותיות אל"ף ולמ"ד
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex unexpectedly has ‘these’ with merkha twice, on alef and lamed.

panels.label: Local note’s Leningrad quotation and description
panels.quote: ל!=אֵ֣לֶּ֣ה (טעם מרכא פעמיים באותיות אל"ף ולמ"ד)
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex unexpectedly has ‘these’ with merkha twice, on alef and lamed.

explanation: The two sources agree with each other. In both printed words, the two accents are munah, although both descriptions call them merkha. This is a shared mismatch between the quoted word and its accent names, not a disagreement between the Introduction and the note.
decision: Confirm the intended accents from the cited reading. If the quoted word is correct, use munah in both descriptions; if merkha is intended, identify the quotation that supports changing its accents.

title: Psalm 1:3 — the illustration lacks the grey maqaf required by the stated policy
issue: Should the verse illustration include the grey maqaf between ‘streams’ and ‘water’?
context: The righteous person is compared to a tree planted beside streams of water. This phrase has an oleh mark on ‘streams’ and a yored mark on ‘water.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — illustration of poetic verse layout
panels.translation: beside streams of water

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — maqaf policy for a two-word oleh and yored
panels.quote: לכן במהדורתנו סימנו אותם כדי שהקורא יבין שיש לצרף את שתי התיבות, אמנם ב{{צבע גופן|אפור|צבע אפור}} כדי שגם ידע שהמקף לא מופיע בכתב־היד.
panels.translation: Therefore, in our edition we marked these maqafs so the reader would understand that the two words should be joined, but in grey so the reader would also know that the maqaf does not appear in the manuscript.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2 — Psalm 1:3 as a manuscript example in the oleh and yored discussion
panels.translation: beside streams of water

explanation: The current verse has a grey maqaf at this boundary, in agreement with the stated policy. The layout illustration has a space. A space is appropriate in the separate manuscript discussion, which explicitly describes Aleppo without maqaf; the question is whether the layout illustration is intended to represent that manuscript form or MAM’s presentation.
decision: If the layout illustration represents MAM, include the grey maqaf. If it deliberately represents the manuscript form, label that distinction.

title: Malachi 2:7 — is the holam dot in the Aleppo example supplied for the reader?
issue: Does the Introduction’s Aleppo example intentionally supply the usual holam dot while documenting only the meteg’s position?
context: The priest is called a messenger of ‘the LORD of hosts.’ Both sources discuss a meteg on the first he of the divine name.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — Malachi 2:7 meteg example
panels.quote: (א!=יְהֹֽוָה־צְבָא֖וֹת): געיה באות ה"א הראשונה של שם הוי"ה
panels.translation: The Aleppo Codex unexpectedly has ‘the LORD of hosts’ with a meteg on the first he of the divine name.

panels.label: Local note’s Aleppo quotation
panels.quote: א!=יְהֽוָה־צְבָא֖וֹת (געיה באות ה"א הראשונה של שם הוי"ה)
panels.translation: The Aleppo Codex unexpectedly has ‘the LORD of hosts’ with a meteg on the first he of the divine name.

panels.label: Local note quoting Yeivin about the absent holam
panels.quote: געיה בה' החלומה אף על פי שהחולם אינו מסומן, מוכיחה שיש כאן הברה
panels.translation: A meteg on the he with the holam vowel, even though the holam is not marked, proves that there is a syllable here.

explanation: The meteg descriptions agree. The Introduction’s example includes a holam dot; the note’s Aleppo quotation lacks it and explicitly explains its absence. The Introduction may use conventional full pointing while illustrating the meteg, rather than claim that Aleppo has that extra dot.
decision: Clarify whether this is an exact Aleppo quotation or a conventionally pointed meteg illustration. Use the same convention consistently, or state why the extra holam dot is supplied.

title: Psalm 119:138 — an initial meteg appears only in the Introduction example
issue: Is the meteg on the initial vav a reading aid in the example, or is it intended as part of the manuscript quotation?
context: The verse describes God’s testimonies as righteous and very faithful. The word in question means ‘and faithfulness.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — Psalm 119:138
panels.quote: (וֶֽאֱמוּנָ֥֗ה): נקודת רביע מיותרת באות נו"ן בנוסף למרכא
panels.translation: ‘And faithfulness’: an extra revia dot on nun, in addition to merkha.

panels.label: Local note’s explicit Aleppo quotation
panels.quote: א!=וֶאֱמוּנָ֥֗ה (נקודת רביע מיותרת באות נו"ן בנוסף למרכא)
panels.translation: The Aleppo Codex unexpectedly has ‘and faithfulness’ with an extra revia dot on nun, in addition to merkha.

explanation: Both sources describe the same extra revia dot. The Introduction also has a meteg on the initial vav; the Aleppo quotation in the note does not. The Introduction’s entry does not explicitly name a manuscript beside its form, so the extra meteg should not automatically be attributed to Aleppo.
decision: Clarify whether the example supplies ordinary reading aids or reproduces a manuscript’s full pointing. If it is a full quotation, identify the source for the initial meteg.

title: Psalm 18:2 — why is a reading attributed to the missing Aleppo pages?
issue: What report of Aleppo supports the attribution beside ‘I love you,’ given that this verse is in the missing part of the codex?
context: David addresses God: ‘I love you, LORD, my strength.’ The local discussion concerns whether the qamats in ‘I love you’ is short or long.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5 — small-qamats examples in Psalms
panels.quote: (א=אֶרְחָמְךָ֖): לכאורה קמץ רחב לפני כללי הדקדוק, אבל המדקדקים הספרדים ציינו מסורת שהקמץ חטוף
panels.translation: Aleppo Codex: ‘I love you.’ The grammatical rules apparently call for a long qamats, but Sephardic grammarians recorded a tradition of short qamats.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4 — the missing section of Psalms
panels.quote: חסרים שני דפים בכתר ארם צובה, שהיו בהם כ-10 מזמורים.
panels.translation: Two pages are missing from the Aleppo Codex; they contained about ten psalms.

panels.label: Local note naming the manuscripts consulted for this word
panels.quote: בכתבי־היד (ל,ש1,ק13,גסטר1) אין געיה בתיבה זו והספק נשאר.
panels.translation: In the Leningrad Codex, Sassoon 1053, Cairo 13, and Gaster 1 there is no meteg in this word, and the uncertainty remains.

explanation: Chapter 4 places the loss between Psalm 15:1 and Psalm 25:1, which includes this verse. The local note discusses reading tradition and other named manuscripts, without supplying an Aleppo report. A prior report or shorthand may explain the chapter 5 attribution; its grammatical discussion alone does not establish that attribution.
decision: Identify the earlier report of Aleppo, or clarify that the form represents a reading tradition or editorial convention rather than a surviving Aleppo reading.

reading_forms.label: MAM’s selected pointing of ‘I love you’

title: Deuteronomy 12:30 — a doubtful manuscript accent or a transcription choice?
issue: Should qadma remain an alternative attributed to the Leningrad Codex when the local note assigns it to the digital transcription?
context: Israel is warned against asking how other nations served their gods. The word ‘saying’ introduces that question.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3 — the two proposed Leningrad readings
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex possibly has ‘saying’ with revia, or with qadma.

panels.label: Local note distinguishing the transcription from the manuscript
panels.quote: הקלדה!=לֵאמֹ֨ר (טעם קדמא) בעקבות BHS, אמנם בכתי"ל נראה שנקודת החולם התחברה לאות מ"ם ולכן נראית כמו קדמא.
panels.translation: The digital transcription unexpectedly has ‘saying’ with qadma, following Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia. In the Leningrad Codex, however, the holam dot appears to have joined the mem, making it look like qadma.

explanation: The Introduction leaves two manuscript readings open. The local note explicitly assigns revia to Leningrad and qadma to the transcription, and explains why the manuscript could look like qadma. These are different descriptions of the remaining uncertainty.
decision: Decide whether the manuscript reading is still unresolved. If it is, preserve both candidates with their evidence; if the note’s interpretation is accepted, label qadma as the transcription reading.

title: Psalm 17:14 — does the first alternative belong to Leningrad?
issue: What supports attributing the first merkha-and-meteg alternative to Leningrad, rather than to the other manuscripts named in the local note?
context: The speaker asks God for deliverance from mortals by God’s hand. The disputed compound contains ‘from mortals’ and ‘your hand.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4 — proposed Leningrad alternatives
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex possibly has: first merkha, then meteg; first meteg, then merkha; or two metegs in the maqaf compound.

panels.label: Local note naming the sources of the first pattern
panels.quote: =ש1,ק13,ל-א,גסטר1 (לגבי מרכא כטעם משני וגעיה בהברה המוטעמת ומקף)
panels.translation: MAM agrees with Sassoon 1053, Cairo 13, St. Petersburg EVR-II-B-55, and Gaster 1 concerning secondary merkha, meteg on the stressed syllable, and maqaf.

panels.label: Local note’s two Leningrad alternatives
panels.quote: ל=<מִֽמְתִ֥ים־יָדְךָ֨׀> (געיה ומרכא ומקף, ואין חטף) לפי המקליד (וכן הוא בקורן בהשמטת המקף), או <מִֽמְתִֽים־יָדְךָ֨׀> (שתיהן געיות) לפי דותן (וכך נראה יותר בכתי"ל).
panels.translation: Leningrad has meteg, merkha, and maqaf, without a hataf vowel, according to the transcriber; Koren has the same accents without maqaf. Alternatively, Dotan interprets both signs as metegs, which seems more likely in the Leningrad Codex.

explanation: The note supports the first accent pattern in other named manuscripts. For Leningrad it records the second pattern from the transcriber and the third from Dotan, favouring the third. The Introduction also offers the first pattern as a Leningrad possibility, without identifying that additional basis.
decision: Identify the report supporting the first Leningrad candidate, or keep it separate as the reading of the other named manuscripts.

title: Psalm 18:7 — merkha in Leningrad, meteg in the transcription
issue: Is meteg still a possible manuscript reading here, or should the Introduction identify it specifically as the digital transcription’s reading?
context: David says that in his distress he calls to God. The disputed word means ‘I call.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4 — possible Leningrad readings
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex possibly has ‘I call’ with merkha and munah, or with meteg and munah.

panels.label: Local note assigning merkha to Leningrad and related sources
panels.translation: Leningrad, St. Petersburg EVR-II-B-55, Gaster 1, and the general practice of Aleppo have ‘I call’ with secondary merkha followed by a hataf vowel.

panels.label: Local note’s digital transcription reading
panels.translation: The digital transcription has ‘I call’ with meteg and a hataf vowel.

explanation: Both alternatives occur in the documentation, but they are assigned differently. The local note attributes merkha to Leningrad and meteg to the transcription. Its appeal to Aleppo’s general practice is not a quotation from a surviving Aleppo page.
decision: Clarify whether the Introduction preserves an unresolved manuscript interpretation or lists the transcription as an alternative source.

reading_forms.label: Leningrad reading attributed by the note

title: Daniel 2:41 — both interpretations remain possible
issue: Should the two readings be labelled separately as the manuscript interpretation and the digital transcription’s still-possible alternative?
context: Daniel describes the statue’s feet as partly clay and partly iron. The expression in question means ‘of iron.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4 — possible Leningrad readings
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex possibly and unexpectedly has ‘of iron’ with meteg and a space, or with merkha and a space.

panels.label: Local note’s manuscript interpretation
panels.quote: ל?=<דִֽי פַרְזְלָ֖א> (געיה וחסר מקף?) לפי הערת ברויאר במהדורת חורב, וכך נראה מעיון בכתב־היד בהגדלה.
panels.translation: Leningrad possibly has ‘of iron’ with meteg and a missing maqaf, according to Breuer’s note in the Horev edition; that is also how it appears on magnified inspection of the manuscript.

panels.label: Local note expressly retaining the transcription alternative
panels.quote: הקלדה=<דִ֥י פַרְזְלָ֖א> (במרכא) בעקבות BHS וגם זה אפשרי.
panels.translation: The digital transcription has ‘of iron’ with merkha, following Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia, and this too is possible.

explanation: The note distinguishes the sources but does not reject the transcription’s merkha interpretation. Both readings lack maqaf, while MAM’s selected reading has maqaf. Describing the transcription as disproved would remove uncertainty that the note explicitly retains.
decision: Keep both possible interpretations, with their source labels, unless additional attributed evidence resolves the short line.

title: Daniel 5:3 — a possible transcription reading is labelled as a manuscript reading
issue: Should the meteg alternative retain the note’s qualification that it may be the Leningrad transcription’s reading?
context: The gold vessels are brought from the temple in Jerusalem. The disputed compound means ‘from the temple.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4 — Leningrad candidate
panels.translation: Leningrad possibly has ‘from the temple’ with meteg and tevir, rather than merkha within the word accented by tevir.

panels.label: Local note’s qualified alternatives
panels.quote:
=ל?,ש1,ק-מ? ושיטת-א (מרכא בתיבת תביר), וכך אצל ברויאר ומג"ה.
ל(הקלדה)?=מִן־הֵֽיכְלָ֛א (געיה ותביר)
panels.translation: MAM agrees with possibly Leningrad, Sassoon 1053, possibly Cambridge Add. 1753, and Aleppo’s general practice in having merkha within the word accented by tevir; Breuer and Miqra’ot Gedolot Ha-keter have the same. A possible Leningrad transcription reading has meteg and tevir.

explanation: The note leaves Leningrad uncertain in both assignments and attaches ‘transcription’ to the meteg candidate. The Introduction preserves the uncertainty but omits that source qualification.
decision: State whether the candidate concerns the manuscript, its transcription, or both. Retain the transcription qualification until a recorded manuscript reading supports removing it.

title: Nehemiah 12:47 — the transcription qualifier is missing from the Introduction
issue: Should the possible meteg reading be identified as the Leningrad transcription’s candidate rather than left as an undifferentiated manuscript reading?
context: Israel provides the singers and gatekeepers with their daily portions. The disputed word means ‘were giving.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4 — Leningrad candidate
panels.translation: Leningrad possibly has ‘were giving’ with meteg and tevir, rather than merkha within the word accented by tevir.

panels.label: Local note’s selected reading and qualified alternative
panels.translation: MAM agrees with Sassoon 1053, possibly Cambridge Add. 1753, British Library Or. 2375, and Aleppo’s general practice in having merkha within the word accented by tevir. The possible Leningrad transcription reading, and possibly Cambridge Add. 1753, have meteg and tevir.

explanation: The local note identifies the possible Leningrad alternative through the transcription and also leaves Cambridge uncertain. The Introduction has the same meteg candidate but drops the transcription qualification. Neither passage settles the manuscript’s short line.
decision: Keep the source qualification, or identify the attributed manuscript reading that justifies a direct Leningrad assignment.

title: Deuteronomy 5:13 — which accent belongs to which Decalogue reading?
issue: What supports assigning munah to the upper reading and merkha to the lower reading?
context: The verse says that the seventh day is a Sabbath ‘to the LORD your God.’ The two accent signs in the Leningrad quotation occur on ‘to the LORD.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3 — allocation to the two Decalogue readings
panels.quote: ל!=(לַיהֹוָ֣֥ה): מונח לטעם העליון לפני מרכא לטעם התחתון
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex unexpectedly has ‘to the LORD’: munah for the upper reading precedes merkha for the lower reading.

panels.label: Local note naming the two signs without allocating them
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex unexpectedly has ‘to the LORD’ with munah and merkha.

explanation: The two signs are confirmed by the local quotation. The Introduction adds an allocation of each sign to a particular Decalogue reading. The local note does not supply that allocation, so agreement on the signs does not also establish the assignment.
decision: Identify an attributed explanation of the two readings that supports the assignment. Otherwise describe the two signs without assigning them to upper and lower readings.

title: Song of Songs 4:16 — is the missing dagesh on zayin, not lamed?
issue: Should the Introduction’s explanation name zayin rather than lamed?
context: The speaker asks the winds to blow through the garden so that its spices may flow. The disputed word means ‘may flow.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4 — Song of Songs 4:16
panels.translation: Leningrad has ‘may flow’: there is no dagesh in lamed.

panels.label: Local note’s Leningrad quotation
panels.translation: Leningrad has ‘may flow’ with a missing dagesh.

explanation: The quoted Leningrad word lacks a dagesh on zayin. MAM’s selected word has that dagesh on zayin; lamed has no dagesh in either word. The note says only ‘missing dagesh,’ while the Introduction specifically names lamed.
decision: Confirm the intended letter. If the compared words are correct, name zayin in the Introduction; if lamed is intended, supply the corresponding quotation.

reading_forms.label: Leningrad word quoted in both passages
MAM’s selected word with dagesh on zayin

title: Lamentations 4:7 — a segol vowel in an example described as qamats
issue: Is the segol vowel in the quoted Leningrad word intentional, or should the proposed qamats reading have a different quotation?
context: The verse says that Zion’s dignitaries were brighter than snow. The disputed word means ‘than snow.’

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4 — Lamentations 4:7
panels.translation: Leningrad possibly and unexpectedly has ‘than snow’: qamats on shin.

panels.label: Local note retaining uncertainty about the dots
panels.quote: ל?!=מִשֶּׁ֔לֶג (קמץ באות שי"ן?); כך לפי ברויאר, אבל בכתב־היד נראה יותר כמו שתי נקודות צמודות מאשר קו של קמץ; וכן דעתו של המקליד.
panels.translation: Leningrad possibly and unexpectedly has ‘than snow’ with qamats on shin, according to Breuer. In the manuscript, however, it looks more like two adjacent dots than a qamats stroke; the transcriber agrees with that view.

explanation: Both printed quotations have a segol vowel on shin, while their explanations discuss qamats. The local note preserves doubt about interpreting the manuscript’s dots; the Introduction’s caption does not retain that question mark. The printed vowel and the proposed manuscript interpretation need separate descriptions.
decision: Clarify which vowel the quotation is intended to represent, and preserve the note’s uncertainty about qamats unless further attributed evidence resolves it.

reading_forms.label: Local note’s word with segol vowel

title: Nehemiah 9:37: should the spelling example include the stress-helper mark?

context: The prayer says that foreign kings rule over the people's bodies and livestock. The example concerns the spelling of the word for “our bodies.”

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4: unusual spellings in the Leningrad Codex
panels.translation: Leningrad: “our bodies,” with the first spelling selected for MAM; the second spelling is the alternative.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4: explanation of the star
panels.quote: הפריט הראשון בכל שורה ברשימה הוא נוסח הכתיב המתאים למסורה והמופיע במהדורתנו ואחריו כוכבית (*)
panels.translation: The first item in each line is the spelling that accords with the Masorah and occurs in our edition, followed by a star.

panels.label: Current MAM text attached to the Nehemiah 9:37 note

decision: Should the Introduction reproduce MAM's complete accentuation here, or explicitly retain this as a spelling-only example?

title: Daniel 7:15: which accent belongs on the rejected spelling of “within”?

panels.label: MAM note on Daniel 7:15: Breuer's spelling
panels.translation: Breuer has “within” without final alef, with munach.

decision: Should the rejected example be tied to a named source with its accentuation, or should the Introduction identify it as a spelling-only illustration?

reading_forms.label: Breuer alternative quoted by the note

title: 2 Kings 15:25: which Leningrad Masorah note supports each spelling?

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4: Leningrad spelling differences
panels.quote: מ"ק-ל תומכת בגירסת המסורה הברורה, אמנם במ"ג-ל יש הערה משובשת התומכת בגירסת כתי"ל.
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex's Masorah Parva supports the clear Masoretic spelling, whereas its Masorah Gedolah has a corrupt note supporting the spelling in the Leningrad text.

panels.label: MAM note on 2 Kings 15:25: Leningrad spelling
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex surprisingly has “and he killed him” with the additional yod.

panels.label: MAM note on 2 Kings 15:25: Masorah support
panels.translation: And the Aleppo, Leningrad, and Tiberian Masorah traditions.

title: Jeremiah 31:27: is the support specifically Aleppo's Masorah Parva?
issue: The Introduction names the Aleppo Codex's Masorah Parva; the verse note names the Aleppo Masorah without identifying the short marginal note.
context: The word “and to plant” is part of God's promise to rebuild Israel and Judah. The competing spelling has an additional vav.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4: Leningrad spelling differences
panels.translation: The selected spelling of “and to plant” is attributed to Aleppo's Masorah Parva; the spelling with the additional vav is attributed to the Leningrad Codex.

panels.label: MAM note on Jeremiah 31:27: selected spelling
panels.translation: MAM agrees with the Aleppo Masorah, and likewise with Breuer and Mikra'ot Gedolot ha-Keter.

explanation: The spelling choice agrees. “Aleppo Masorah” does not specify whether the evidence is in the short marginal notes, the longer notes, or another Masoretic list.
decision: Should the Introduction keep the more specific Masorah Parva attribution with its supporting reference, or say simply “Aleppo Masorah,” as the note does?

title: Ecclesiastes 1:17: what supports the exclamation mark on Leningrad's spelling?
issue: The Introduction's exclamation mark asserts a conflict with the Leningrad Codex's Masorah, but the verse note discusses the written spelling without citing that Masorah conflict.
context: The speaker seeks to understand wisdom, madness, and folly. The example concerns “madness,” with the vav in different positions in the competing spellings.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4: meaning of the exclamation mark
panels.quote: ואחריו סימן קריאה (!) במקרים שבהם הכתיב בכתי"ל סותר את הערות המסורה שבתוך כתי"ל עצמו.
panels.translation: An exclamation mark follows in cases where the spelling in the Leningrad Codex contradicts the Masorah notes within that same codex.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4: Ecclesiastes spelling list
panels.translation: Selected spelling of “madness”; the Leningrad alternative has an exclamation mark.

panels.label: MAM note on Ecclesiastes 1:17: Leningrad spelling
panels.quote: ל=הוֹלֵל֖וֹת (כתיב מלא וי"ו וחסר וי"ו), וכן בדותן ובהקלדה.

explanation: The note explains why the Leningrad spelling differs from Breuer's report. It does not identify a Leningrad Masorah note contradicting that spelling. The exclamation mark therefore adds a separate claim beyond the spelling comparison.
decision: Should the exclamation mark remain with an explicit reference to the conflicting Leningrad Masorah note, or be omitted if the entry is only a spelling comparison?

title: Daniel 5:16: what supports the Leningrad attribution for “the chain”?
issue: The Introduction attributes both the pointed written spelling and the spoken spelling to Leningrad, but the verse's notes do not document that attribution for this word.
context: The king offers Daniel a gold chain for interpreting the writing. The Introduction gives a ketiv, the written spelling, and a qere, the spoken spelling, for “the chain.”

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 4: difficult spelling decisions
panels.translation: Leningrad: “and the chain,” with the first spelling labelled ketiv and the second qere; the example is selected for MAM.

explanation: The distinction between written and spoken spelling is explicit. The notes attached to this verse discuss other words, rather than identifying the Leningrad evidence for this pointed ketiv and qere.
decision: Should this entry retain the explicit Leningrad attribution with a supporting source, or distinguish the selected MAM spellings from what is directly documented for Leningrad?

title: Deuteronomy 12:20 and 28:49: do spelling examples also promise MAM's meteg marks?

context: Deuteronomy 12:20 concerns God enlarging Israel's territory. Deuteronomy 28:49 describes a nation coming from far away. These are examples in a list about consonantal spelling.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3: Deuteronomy spelling list, 12:20

panels.translation: Your territory, preceded by the direct-object marker.

panels.translation: From far away.

In 28:49 the Introduction's selected example lacks MAM's initial meteg. The list's explanation identifies the star with spelling, so these differences need not be claims about complete pointing.
decision: Should the selected spelling examples reproduce all MAM marks, or should the Introduction say that their accents and meteg marks are illustrative?

title: Numbers 1:10 and 10:19: should the Leningrad spacing still have question marks?
issue: The Introduction gives uncertain alternatives for joining the names Pedahzur and Zurishaddai, while the current notes describe the Leningrad spellings directly.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3: compound names, Numbers 1:10
panels.translation: Selected Pedahzur as one word, possibly supported by Leningrad; an alternative of two spaced words is also tentatively attributed to Leningrad.

panels.label: MAM note on Numbers 1:10
panels.quote: ("פדהצור" תיבה אחת); בכל כתבי־היד האלה אין מקף ואין שווא מתחת לאות ה"א

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3: compound names, Numbers 10:19

reading_forms.label: Leningrad quotation in the current note

title: Deuteronomy 32:6: should the Leningrad quotation include the yod's sheva?

panels.quote: ל=הֲ־לַיְהוָה֙ (חטף פתח באות ה"א, תיבות מוקפות, פתח באות למ"ד ושווא באות יו"ד)

title: Isaiah 44:14: which Aleppo Masorah source calls for a small final nun?

title: Psalm 27:13: which manuscript's Masorah supports the six dots on “unless”?

panels.translation: Leningrad and Sassoon 1053 have “unless” with a dot above and a dot below each of the two lamed letters and the alef, in accordance with Aleppo's Masorah Parva.

explanation: The quoted Leningrad dot pattern agrees. The specific Masorah attribution differs: Leningrad in the Introduction, Aleppo in the note. Both manuscripts could have supporting notes, so this is not evidence that one attribution is false.

title: Psalm 77:8, Ruth 3:13, and Esther 1:6: what else should a letter-size example include?

panels.translation: Spend the night.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5: Esther 1:6 letter-size example
panels.translation: “White fabric,” with the selected large het.

panels.translation: White fabric.

title: Exodus 7:13: does the note attribute the yod meteg to Leningrad?
issue: The Introduction's Leningrad quotation lacks meteg, while the note's opening agreement includes Leningrad beside MAM's word with meteg.
context: The verse says that Pharaoh's heart hardened. The disputed meteg is beneath the yod in “and it hardened.”

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3: light meteg examples
panels.translation: Leningrad has “and it hardened,” without meteg.

panels.label: Current MAM text attached to the Exodus 7:13 note
panels.translation: And it hardened.

panels.translation: British Library Or. 4445, Sassoon 507, Cairo 18, and the Washington Pentateuch have light meteg beneath the yod.

title: Jeremiah 48:20 and 50:6: are the hataf examples written spellings or spoken spellings?
issue: The Introduction labels both examples as Aleppo qere, while the notes attribute the hataf to Aleppo's pointed ketiv.

panels.label: MAM note on Jeremiah 48:20

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5: Jeremiah hataf list, 50:6
panels.translation: Aleppo qere: “led them astray,” with a hataf.

panels.label: MAM note on Jeremiah 50:6
panels.translation: Aleppo's pointed ketiv has the written counterpart of “led them astray,” with a hataf.

explanation: The consonants at the ends of the quoted words differ, as do the ketiv/qere labels. The notes document the hataf on the written spellings. MAM's spoken spellings do not independently establish that Aleppo supplied those same pointed qere spellings.
decision: Should the Introduction quote the pointed ketiv documented in the notes, or explicitly explain why the manuscript's ketiv vowel is being illustrated on the qere spelling?

title: Ezekiel 17:17: which codex has the hataf in “siege ramp”?
issue: The Introduction names Leningrad for this hataf; the verse note names Aleppo.

panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex has “siege ramp” with a hataf.

panels.label: MAM note on Ezekiel 17:17
panels.translation: The Aleppo Codex has “siege ramp” with a hataf.

panels.label: MAM note on Proverbs 30:17: a second word
panels.translation: The Leningrad Codex has “obedience to a mother” with a hataf.

title: Deuteronomy 20:1: did Dotan describe the seder mark as erroneous or uncertain?
issue: The Introduction says Dotan marked this seder as an error; the verse note says he bracketed it as uncertain.
context: The verse begins “When you go out to war.” A seder mark identifies the beginning of a reading division. The Leningrad Codex's mark here is absent from the lists of reading divisions cited by both passages.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3: reading divisions in Deuteronomy
panels.translation: Dotan marked it as an error: {seder}.

panels.label: MAM note on Deuteronomy 20:1
panels.quote: דותן הביא אותו בסוגריים כסדר מסופק: {ס}.
panels.translation: Dotan included it in brackets as an uncertain seder: {seder}.

panels.label: MAM note on Deuteronomy 20:1: proposed explanation
panels.quote: וייתכן שהסדר צויין כאן בטעות בגלל הפסוק הדומה בסדר שמתחיל בראש פרשת "כי תצא".

title: Which text do the Introduction's dehi and oleh-weyored totals describe?
issue: The Introduction's totals differ from the corresponding counts in current MAM, and it does not identify a different text or counting rule for them.
context: The figures concern poetic verses in Psalms, Proverbs, and Job: verses with dehi, and verses whose principal division is attributed to oleh-weyored. A verse count is different from counting every accent sign.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2: stress marking for dehi and tsinnor
panels.quote: מתוך 2685 פסוקי אמ"ת המוטעמים בטעם הדחי.
panels.translation: Out of 2,685 poetic verses in Psalms, Proverbs, and Job accented with dehi.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2: oleh-weyored
panels.quote: מתוך 4465 פסוקי אמ"ת, רק 421 מתחלקים בחלוקה ראשית ע"י עולה ויורד (כ-9.4%).
panels.translation: Of 4,465 poetic verses in Psalms, Proverbs, and Job, only 421 have their principal division made by oleh-weyored, about 9.4 percent.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2: oleh and yored in two words
panels.quote: עולה ויורד מוטעם בשתי תיבות ב-55 פסוקים, שהם כ-13% מתוך 421 פסוקים המוטעמים ע"י עולה ויורד.
panels.translation: Oleh-weyored is accented in two words in 55 verses, about 13 percent of the 421 verses accented with oleh-weyored.

explanation: The existing current-MAM results give 2,679 verses containing dehi and 423 containing oleh. The 55 verses with oleh and yored in different words agree with the Introduction's list. The older totals could reflect another text, an earlier version, or a distinction in what counts as a principal division; the quoted passages do not say which.
decision: Should these figures explicitly count current MAM verses under a stated rule, or remain figures for another identified text or definition? In particular, does “principal division” exclude any of the 423 current verses containing oleh?

title: Isaiah 44:24: is the maqaf part of the Leningrad quotation or a reading aid?

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5: unusual pointing of the ketiv
panels.translation: “From me,” with two written words joined by maqaf; the qere has “from me” as one word.

panels.label: MAM note on Isaiah 44:24: Aleppo ketiv

panels.translation: Aleppo has “faint,” with a qamats dot under lamed.

title: Proverbs 8:34: why does the design example use galgal without the stated uncertainty?
issue: The design list has galgal and a certain Aleppo attribution, while the other Introduction entry and the note have atnah hafukh and uncertainty about the oleh mark.
context: Wisdom calls the person who listens to her happy. The words are “listening to me.” The uncertainty concerns whether the oleh mark belongs over mem or ayin.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5: unusual Aleppo vowels and accents, Proverbs
panels.translation: Aleppo may have “listening to me” with the oleh mark over ayin, selected for MAM, or with the oleh mark over mem.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 5: poetic accent design, maqaf between oleh and yored
panels.translation: Aleppo: “listening to me,” with galgal and the starred example.

panels.label: MAM note on Proverbs 8:34
panels.quote: א?=שֹׁמֵ֢֫עַֽ לִ֥י (סימן ה"עולה" תלוי בין האותיות מ"ם ועי"ן)
panels.translation: Aleppo may have “listening to me” with the oleh mark over mem; the oleh mark is suspended between mem and ayin.

explanation: The two marks below mem are different accents, not merely different ordering of the same signs. The Introduction's separate explanation distinguishes galgal from atnah hafukh. The design list also lacks the question mark retained in the other entry. Its example of two independently accented words remains understandable, but the quotation and certainty do not match the other passage.
decision: Should the design example use atnah hafukh and retain the uncertainty stated in the other entry, or explain a different intended notation and attribution?

reading_forms.label: Uncertain Aleppo quotation in the note

title: Psalm 68:18: should the revia example include the explicitly retained rafe?
issue: The revia list omits a rafe that the Introduction's rafe section and the verse note explicitly include.
context: The psalm speaks of God's chariots and the Lord among them. The word “among them” has a rafe over bet, marking it as undageshed.

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 2: rafe

title: Deuteronomy 31:21: a repeated vowel-dispute link points to verse 50

panels.label: Introduction, chapter 3: Accuracy of the Leningrad Codex's vowels
panels.translation: In the second case (Deuteronomy 31:21). The repeated link targets 31:50.

panels.label: Doc-note at Deuteronomy 31:21

explanation: The paragraph's first reference already points to 31:21. The note about this vowel dispute is also at 31:21; the repeated destination is the inconsistent part.
decision: Make the repeated link point to Deuteronomy 31:21, retaining the existing discussion of the two vowel readings.

title: Genesis 9:29: a chapter 9 link carries a chapter 6 destination
